name: Sux4J (GOV / GOV3Function minimal perfect hash)
workload: 1 billion random 64-bit integer keys; lookup (evaluation) time and space (bits/key) for Sux4J's GOV minimal perfect hash function compared against CMPH's CHD (λ=4,5,6), EMPHF, BBHash, RecSplit and PTHash, as reproduced in the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper's Table 5 and mirrored in the roberto-trani/mphf_benchmark README.
claimed_speedup: GOV: 175 ns/key lookup, 2.23 bits/key, 875s construction vs CHD (CMPH) 416-419 ns/key at 2.01-2.17 bits/key across λ=4..6 -> GOV lookup is about 2.4x faster than CMPH's CHD at similar-to-worse space (derived from page data: 419/175≈2.4, 416/175≈2.4)
compiler_and_flags: C++ harness built with CMake Release per repo instructions; GOV/Sux4J itself runs on a JVM whose exact version/flags are not stated in either source
hardware: Intel Core i9-9900K @ 3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: GOV uses more space than CHD (2.23 vs 2.01-2.17 bits/key) despite being ~2.4x faster to look up; GOV construction (875s for 1B keys) is much slower than BBHash (100-253s) though far faster than CHD (1972-23746s); JVM overhead vs native C/C++ libraries is not isolated in these numbers.
caveats: The GOV row in the comparison table is reproduced from the PTHash paper's Table 5, not independently re-run inside the roberto-trani/mphf_benchmark C++ harness (its own README says GOV is excluded from its reproducible build commands because it is Java-based); exact JVM version/flags for the original GOV measurement are not given in either source.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "Sux4J" --limit 10; cross-checked via gh api repos/roberto-trani/mphf_benchmark/readme

name: minperf (RecSplit implementation)
workload: 100,000 randomly generated long keys (default `size` in PerformanceTest.java); RecSplit-based MPHF evaluation (lookup) time and space, per the author's own micro-benchmark, recorded as a comment alongside the code comparing it to CHD and GOV.
claimed_speedup: Source comment in PerformanceTest.java: 'CHD: 2.25 bits/key, 182 nanoseconds/key' vs minperf's RecSplit (leafSize=11, averageBucketSize=55): '1.97 bits/key, 163 nanoseconds/key evaluation time' -> roughly 10% faster lookup than CMPH's CHD at smaller space (1.97 vs 2.25 bits/key) (verbatim from code comment)
tradeoffs: Numbers are hand-written code comments from a prior run rather than logged/automated benchmark output; no hardware, JVM version, or full dataset description is stated; the project's README says a paper was planned but the repo has been inactive since 2021 and no paper was ever added.
caveats: CHD/GOV comparison numbers are code comments (author's own recollection of past results), not generated by an automated report in this repo; no compiler/JVM/CPU stated, so the comparison cannot be independently reproduced from the repo alone.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "minimal perfect hash" language:Java --limit 15

name: mph (Go, Hash-Displace-Compress / CHD)
workload: Lookups over a 102k-word dictionary using string keys; MPH Table.Lookup (CHD algorithm, Murmur3 hash) vs a Go map[string]uint32, via `go test -bench`.
claimed_speedup: 'Lookups on that dictionary take about 30ns and are 27% faster than a map[string]uint32': BenchmarkTable-12 29.99 ns/op vs BenchmarkTableMap-12 40.92 ns/op (verbatim + derived from page data: 1-29.99/40.92≈27%)
compiler_and_flags: go.mod declares `go 1.17`; the exact Go toolchain version/build flags used for the quoted benchmark run are not stated in the README
tradeoffs: Build/construction takes 18ms for a 102k-word dictionary and requires all keys known upfront; the table is read-only after construction; no comparison is given against other Go hash-map variants or sync.Map.
caveats: Go compiler version and exact build flags for the quoted ns/op numbers are not stated (only the '-12' GOMAXPROCS suffix and the CPU model are given); the numbers are first-party and have not been independently reproduced elsewhere.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "minimal perfect hash" --sort stars --limit 30

name: go-mph (Go, Hash-Displace-Compress)
workload: 16-key toy protocol-command lookup table, and the 235,000-word /usr/dict/words dictionary; go-mph (hash/displace MPHF) lookups vs Go's built-in map, as described in the author's Gopher Academy Advent 2017 blog post.
claimed_speedup: 'My implementation is about 25% faster than using a regular Go map for 16 keys and 50% faster when testing with the 235,000 entries in /usr/dict/words.' (verbatim from blog post; no raw ns/op table is given for this specific comparison — a separate ns/op table earlier on the same page, 20.4 vs 172 ns/op, benchmarks an unrelated toy multiplicative hash function, not go-mph, and must not be conflated with it)
tradeoffs: Construction for the 235k-word set takes 100-125ms and needs all keys upfront; uses 8 bytes/entry (index + seed), far more than the same author's companion project go-boomphf (~3.7 bits/entry), which trades speed (only 'a tiny bit faster than a regular Go map') for much lower memory use.
caveats: The 25%/50% figures are prose claims in a blog post with no accompanying raw benchmark numbers, CPU model, or Go version for this specific comparison.
found_via: WebSearch: "dgryski go-mph OR go-boomphf minimal perfect hash benchmark blog ns/op" -> https://blog.gopheracademy.com/advent-2017/mphf/

name: zmph (Zig comptime minimal perfect hash map)
workload: 100,000 lookups against a compile-time-generated key set; ZMPH perfect-hash map vs Zig std.StringHashMap and std.StaticStringMap, measured with zbench via `zig build benchmark --release=fast`.
claimed_speedup: ZMPH Lookup 26ns avg (min 18ns) vs StringHashMap Lookup 45ns avg (~1.7x faster) and vs StaticStringMap Lookup 10.4µs avg (~400x faster); ZMPH build 28.872ms avg vs StringHashMap build 6.1ms avg (ZMPH ~5x slower to build) and StaticStringMap build 2.029ms avg (~14x slower to build) (verbatim + derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Construction (build) is far slower than the hash maps it's compared against (~5-14x), so ZMPH only pays off for read-heavy, rarely-rebuilt static tables; requires the key set to be known at compile time (comptime); repo has no LICENSE file.
caveats: No LICENSE file, so reuse status is unclear (treat as all-rights-reserved until the author adds one); benchmark run on a single personal laptop CPU with no independent reproduction; project is very new/low-visibility (8 stars, single author) and numbers are self-reported.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "minimal perfect hash" language:Zig --limit 10
